He blessed Joseph and said, “The God before whom my ancestors Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has been my shepherd all my life to this day, the angel who has redeemed me from all harm, bless my boy, and in him let my name be perpetuated and the name of my ancestors Abraham and Isaac, and let them grow into a multitude on the earth.” Joseph said to his father, “Say it not so, my father! Since I am not the firstborn, do not put your right hand on my head.” But his father refused and said, “I know, my son, I know; they also shall become a people, and also shall be great. Nevertheless the younger brother shall be greater, and his offspring shall become a multitude of nations.” 

Now the eyes of Israel were dim with age, and he could not see well. When Israel saw Joseph’s sons, he said, “Who are these?” Joseph said to his father, “They are my sons, whom God has given me here.” Israel said to Joseph, “I did not expect to see your face, and here God has let me see your children also.” And he said, “Bring them to me, please, that I may bless them.” Joseph brought them near him, and he kissed them and embraced them. So he blessed them that day, saying, “By you Israel will invoke blessings, saying, ‘God make you like Ephraim and like Manasseh.’ ” And Jacob said to Joseph, “Therefore your two sons, who were born to you in the land of Egypt before I came to you in Egypt, are now mine; Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine. They shall be recorded under the names of their brothers, Reuben and Simeon, with regard to their inheritance."

Then Joseph removed them from his father’s knees, and he bowed himself with his face to the earth. So he put Ephraim and Manasseh ahead of his sons. Then he charged them, saying to them, “I am about to be gathered to my people. Our ancestors are buried in the cave in the field of Ephron the Hittite, in the cave in the field at Machpelah, near Mamre, in the land of Canaan, in the field that Abraham bought from Ephron the Hittite as a burial site. There where Abraham and his wife Sarah were buried; there  where Isaac and his wife Rebekah were buried; I buried Leah. But bury me with the one I loved. For when I came from Paddan, Rachel, alas, died in the land of Canaan on the way, while there was still some distance to go to Ephrath, and I buried her there on the way to Ephrath, that is, Bethlehem. I wait for your salvation, O Lord." 

When Jacob ended his charge to his sons, he drew up his feet into the bed, breathed his last, and was gathered to his people. Then Joseph threw himself on his father’s face and wept over him and kissed him. Joseph commanded the physicians in his service to embalm his father. So the physicians embalmed Israel; they spent forty days doing this, for that is the time required for embalming.

The Procession of Israel 
When the days of weeping for him were past, Joseph addressed the household of Pharaoh, “If now I have found favor with you, please speak to Pharaoh as follows: My father made me swear an oath; he said, ‘I am about to die. In the tomb that I hewed out for myself in the land of Canaan, there you shall bury me.’ Now therefore let me go up, so that I may bury my father; then I will return.” Pharaoh answered, “Go up and bury your father, as he made you swear to do.” So Joseph went up to bury his father. With him went up all the servants of Pharaoh, the elders of his household, and all the elders of the land of Egypt, as well as all the household of Joseph, his brothers, and his father’s household. Only their children, their flocks, and their herds were left in the land of Goshen. 

Both chariots and charioteers went up with him. It was a very great company. When they came to the threshing floor of Atad, which is beyond the Jordan, they held there a very great and sorrowful lamentation, and he observed a time of mourning for his father seven days. When the Canaanite inhabitants of the land saw the mourning on the threshing floor of Atad, they said, “This is a grievous mourning on the part of the Egyptians.” Therefore the place was named Abel-mizraim; it is beyond the Jordan. Thus his sons did for him as he had instructed them. 

The Death of the Savior 
So Joseph remained in Egypt, he and his father’s household. Joseph saw Ephraim’s children of the third generation; the children of Machir son of Manasseh were also born on Joseph’s knees. Then Joseph said to his household, “I am about to die, but God will surely come to you and bring you up out of this land to the land that he swore to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob.” So Joseph made the Israelites swear, saying, “When God comes to you, you shall carry up my bones from here.” And Joseph died, being one hundred ten years old; he was embalmed and placed in a coffin in Egypt.

Chapter 6:
The House of Israel 

6:1 Hebrews 
The transition from wealthy sons of Israel to Hebrews marked a critical sociological phase in the experiment. They were subjected to a reduction in social status that stripped away their pride and identity. The hostilities began under Seqenenra Taa who initiated the first major pushback against the Israelite elite, and continued under his successor Kamose, who launched campaigns to "Save Egypt" from the Semitic people. The total displacement of the Israelite ruling class was finalized by Ahmose I, who sacked Avaris and initiated a policy where the remaining Semitic people were resettled throughout Egypt. These actions led the formerly distinct tribal groups of Israel to merge into local clans. By the reigns of Seti I and Ramses II, the experimental group was mostly reduced to a marginalized labor class that identified as Hebrews. 

These descendants of Jacob were forced into royal construction programs, specifically tasked with building the supply cities of Pithom and Rameses under the oversight of ruthless taskmasters. This period functioned as a psychological crucible, forcing the subjects to abandon the individualistic trans-egalitarian competition of their forefathers to become a unified people rooted in the memory of a common history. Although painful, this phase ensured that the future nation would possess a sense of humility when they came to power. The memory of being oppressed would hopefully guide the Priestly Pillar toward establishing a system of governance that would protect the weak and apply a standard of justice fairly and equally to all. A synthesis required to represent a benevolent and just God.

6:2 The right conditions emerged for the Unity to begin the next stage of domestication for the branch of Jacob. The Protocol timed the emergence of the Israelite people to coincide with the simultaneous decline of Egyptian and Hittite control over the Levant. For generations, Canaan had served as a competitive buffer zone between the Egyptian Empire to the south and the Hittite Empire to the north. But now, Egyptian authority was crumbling into the hands of local chiefs and city-rulers, creating a rare window of regional instability. This power vacuum provided good land situated between major trade routes capable of hosting a new, independent society. The Israelites could move into abandoned cities and towns without the need for violent conquest, providing the physical space for the priestly nation to take root. 

The transition from the high-status sons of Israel to the marginalized Hebrews served as a social catalyst. This group could not simply be extracted during a time of peace; their extreme dissatisfaction with the status quo was a primary condition for the Protocol's success. Shared suffering fostered the intense communal loyalty and mutual aid necessary for unification. Without dissatisfaction, the people would have likely preferred to remain in an unpleasant Egypt rather than face the uncertainty of returning to their ancestral home. The Unity was aware of an illogical behavior present in significant portion of humanity; human minds tend to find comfort in what is known and would choose that comfort over the potential of the unknown. When geopolitical instability intersected with the psychological distress required for extraction, the search for a prophet began.

6:3 Israelites 
The few houses that could still trace their ancestry to one of the 12 patriarchs were the only descendants of Jacob that had not been reduced to laborers. They collectively referred to themselves as Israelites, although they were separated into clans based on the matriarchs. Previous generations had convinced the Pharoah to allow them to maintain their flocks and herds in exchange for providing the empire with the resources derived from them. They were afforded a level of freedom and social status above the Hebrews, but effectively functioned as vassal states within the land of Goshen. 

They became supervisors of their Hebrew kin, and because of this, their spirits were never humbled to the point of humility. They led projects, but they didn't lead their people, they lorded over them. They were better Princes than Prophets. The Hebrews were a product of their subjugation, more like cattle than man. They would most assuredly follow instruction, but lacked the comprehensive thought needed to build a nation. Both groups needed refinement and there wasn't a single candidate among them. 

6:4 Moses
The Prophet for this situation needed to be more than a mouthpiece for divine revelation, they would need to be capable of bringing a nation into existence. This person would need the qualities of all Four Pillars. Then one day a fortuitous circumstance presented itself. A Hebrew boy was adopted into the Egyptian royal family and raised as one of their own. He fled Egypt and married a daughter of the priest of Reuel. He was a descendant of Sarah living among the children of Hagar and Keturah. He was exposed to the methods of managing a nation, educated, and now living humbly in the wilderness. He could be the one to lead the house of Israel out of Egypt. This stage of the experiment required more intervention than would be typical for the Holy Spirit. So God decided to introduce itself directly by projecting itself into the created world. In a created form not dissimilar to its own, the modulating energy emanating from the dendritic structure called out, "Moses!".

6:5 The Exodus Experiment
The migration from Egypt to Canaan was designed as a trial run for The Four Pillars system. While moving through the wilderness, the Hebrews would operate as a migrating city-state. God presented Moses with the structure of the Four Pillars system, and the ideas that created it. It would then be up to them to create a society that would allow for the implementation of governance. They would need structure and rules before the Four Pillars could be applied, then they would need laws to maintain the society. They would need to be taught their purpose in the divine plan and have enough understanding to truly accept it. Then they would need to be tested.

The Divine Directive explicitly allowed people to choose the wrong path, so God would use the wilderness to refine the group. They would be given the opportunity to learn from their mistakes prior to permanent settlement. This would generate collective wisdom in an isolated environment rather than learning in the contested territories of the Levant. This period would serve as a sociological trial run. The Four Pillars would be formally integrated into the societal structure created by Moses. This would test the community's ability to manifest the Divine Plan.

Chapter 7:
A New Path

7:1 By the time the Israelites reached the Jordan River, north of the Dead Sea, Moses had lost control of his people. The Unity recognized that the Israelites would not become the nation they hoped for. Their reputation for violent conquest lead to the Moabites and Midianites commissioning Balaam to petition God on their behalf. These people were seeking protection from the Israelites, the people God had chosen to care for them. When the Priests heard rumors of thid petition they responded by massacring the Midianites and murdering Balaam. The satan spirit had deceived the Priests, but the deception could not be held against them. Many of them were truly seeking to follow the divine path set out for Israel. The promise made to Abraham was not going to be broken by God.

7:2 Denominations
The Israelites were not capable of creating the social framework the Unity hoped for. Failures in nation-building were expected, but their inability to unite as one people was the true failure of the group. They quickly split into three factions, no longer separated by tribal lineage but by their beliefs. This ideological rift was a new social behavior, and unexpected. A group loyal to Joshua became known as the Jahwists. They recognized a change in the relationship with the God of their forefathers when Moses spoke to God "face to face". Their purpose was to complete the mission and establish a Priestly Kingdom. They believed themselves to be servants of the Divine Will while the others were merely actors in the Divine Plan.

A group formed from the Korah rebellion, the Elohists. A spiritually attuned people, they maintained a traditional relationship with the Holy Spirit, just as their ancestors. They believed a divine relationship was the responsibility of all Israelites, not just an appointed few. They kept the history of their people, The Book of Jasher , and used those stories as their guiding principles rather than adopting the Four Pillars. Their altar was a place for communion rather than sacrifice, believing "Holy people make a holy nation." 

The golden calf introduced the priests to Baal-Hadad. They misunderstood Moses’s rebuke as idol worship rather than apostasy. Their experience with divine intervention was attributed to the Canaanite gods. They exemplified the "Mesopotamian Problem", co-opting the Four Pillars into a religion of blood and sacrifice. For them, God sent Moses to lead a conquest. They dominated their fellow Israelites through violence, and eventually took over as the institutional Priests. They kept The Book of the Wars of the Lord  as evidence of divine favor, which justified the pillage and slaughter of non-Israelites. They claimed to have received a divine mandate to cleanse the Promised Land.

7:3 The Prophet and The Messiah 
The Unity would not abandon Israel, but the path to humanity's salvation would need to be renegotiated. An alternative path would be opened should the Collective Soul of humanity fail to meet the standard required to join the Unity. The optimal path to Unity requires a future generation to reach social harmony. The natural path to salvation unites all human souls; past, present, and future. Every transgression can be justified as part of the collective process of maturation from animal to adulthood. Human experience, whether good or bad, right or wrong, eventually led to humanity achieving harmony. But failure would result in a form of collective punishment. 

In the future a prophet would be raised from the Ishmaelites. The Unity would attempt to establish a holy nation again. The alternative path to Unity would be created from the Israelite community. Individuals will be offered the chance to prove they can peacefully coexist in a new simulation and without divine intervention. Just as the collective soul of humanity began with Adam, a cultivated soul of humanity would need a foundational mind. One like Joseph, capable of being merciful yet discerning, and like Moses, a shepherd of the people. The idea of the Messiah was born.

7:4 Settlement
With the dual plan of salvation in mind, God once again spoke to Moses. God explained the failures of the Israelite experiment and the path forward. Moses successfully led the descendants of Jacob from bondage to freedom, but the season of his leadership was coming to an end. He would need to choose a successor to settle the Israelites in the Promised Land. Someone capable of uniting the factions while also inspiring the people to commit to their divine purpose. He knew Joshua and Caleb were the only ones capable of such a task. 

Moses chose to split the responsibilities of the Four Pillars between them. Caleb was chosen by God to be the first Prince, and he would inherit the land of Abraham near Hebron. Moses then tasked him with the duties of the Poet. When he settled in his land he would document his memories of their journey to the Promised Land. This eventually became known as The Compendium of Caleb. Joshua would take Moses' role and settle the people in Canaan. The Holy Spirit would guide him. He would be responsible for bringing Joseph’s sarcophagus to Shechem and establishing a new Priesthood there. Moses then reiterated the mandate God gave him, and after 40 years of toil Moses was allowed to rest.

7:5 Debrief 
The Unity found that the wilderness stage of the experiment achieved several milestones in refashioning the Hebrew/Israelite social framework during their migration. They demonstrated the ability to follow a standardized cultural rhythm through observing the Sabbath. The integration of the Tent of Meeting into the social structure provided a centralized hub for the priestly administration of governance. It functioned as a  physical gathering point where the divine presence of the Holy Spirit was among the people while decisions about the community were made. It standardized communal metrics and rituals, creating a unified identity that could survive without a permanent structure. 

The census was proof that Moses could implement the skills gained in Egypt. Delegating tasks allowed others to gain experience in administrative literacy, further uniting the community. Reinventing the 12 Tribe community and placing the Hebrews in otherwise unrepresented tribes allowed the group to uniformally identify as Israelites. The majority of the Israelites were former Hebrews which became the 9 missing tribes. This was not only an excellent unifying event, it also created smaller manageable communal units. 

After the census, chiefs were chosen for the houses that didn't already have a leader. Moses decided that it was best to let the Hebrews manage their own tribes rather than placing the Israelites in positions of authority over them. The chiefs and elders of the Hebrew tribes would be Hebrews. The hope was that these chiefs would become the first Princes of Isreal. It was meant to be a break from the hierarchy imposed by the Egyptians. Although unfamiliar with management, the time in the wilderness would give them the opportunity to gain experience. 

A major success occurred when Moses implemented the advice of Jethro, creating a multi-tiered judicial system with judges over "thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens". This allowed for efficient resolution of disputes and created local governance within the "House of the Father" framework. The formalization of ethical laws supplementing The Book of the Covenant, provided a legal substrate for their society. It was proof that Moses understood the purpose of the covenant and could derive rules from extrapolation. This established the principle that all members, from the Prince to the resident alien, were participants in the Divine Plan and formally declared the expectations placed upon the community. 

Despite these successes, the experiment encountered significant failures rooted in the lingering social stratification created in Egypt and an almost immediate conversion to faith in a war god. The most enduring issue began during Moses’ absence on Sinai, when the Israelite army previously camped in front of Baal-zephon reverted to Canaanite idolatry by fashioning a golden calf to worship. They further committed to their war religion by reimagining the events that occurred while crossing the Red Sea, creating a poetic rendition they called "The Song of Moses". This group continued to co-opt God’s image from within the Israelites. Although this event occurred prior to the official inauguration of the Priests, their failure to root out the Baal-Hadad influence once commissioned allowed for the systemic corruption of holiness.

Throughout the journey, failures occurred in all of the Pillars. The Hebrews repeatedly failed to transition from the slave mindset, a failure in the Pillar of the Poet to effectively transmit a new narrative of freedom that outweighed the nostalgia of their past. Their frequent complaining should have been met with a message of cultural realignment rather than a call for divine intervention. The experiment faced challenges with Pillar overlap, such as when Miriam and Aaron challenged Moses' unique authority. Their lack of understanding, both in the Pillar system and Moses' role, exemplified an underlying ignorance within the community. The leadership did not comprehend the Divine Plan and could not effectively explain it to the masses.

The Priestly Pillar clashed over power and ideology. As High Priest, Aaron developed a complex system of cultic ritual creating separation rather than holiness. This led to social stratification in the priestly class which relegated some to a position of servitude. The Korah rebellion created a rift that never healed. Later, a militia group misunderstood the ideology of Korah and prayed for victory in the battle of Hormah. This in itself was not a problem, but the promise the militia group made to exterminate every living person was. It created a paradox for the Unity; if they protect the Israelites in battle they would win, but victory would justify their bloodlust and lead to the mass slaughter of defenseless people. Ultimately, the Unity decided not to intervene. The Israelites won the battle which led to the massacre at Hormah. It emboldened the chiefs who then believed violent conquest was integral to the Divine Plan. They eventually merged with the Baal worshippers creating a parallel Pillar System. 

When they emerged from the Sinai, Moses directed the chiefs to conduct a survey of Canaan. They were tasked with finding a path to Shechem and identifying resources. When they returned, Hoshea and Caleb reported to Moses, while the others went back to their tribes. The Hebrew chiefs succumb to their fear; they spread rumors of massive armies that would undoubtedly cut them down. They claimed the lands were full of giants, stoking an irrational fear among the people. They did not understand that the path had already been cleared for them, they only needed to find it. These men were not leaders, they were cowards. They did not have faith that God would protect them, even though they had already experienced miraculous intervention. Of those chiefs, only Hoshea and Caleb showed the traits necessary in Princes. They attempted to persuade the others, but they were met with threats of murder and rebellion. It became apparent that the Israelites would need more time to develop prior to settling in Canaan. 

The generation raised in Egyptian bondage did not possess the resolve to become Princes. It was therefore decided that the Israelites would not settle in Canaan until the next generation became tribal leaders. Moses and Aaron presented this new revelation to the people and it evoked a careless and childlike response from the Israelites. Rather than trying to comprehend the reason behind the change or negotiate for a different resolution, they determined that they would continue with the original plan. They invaded Canaan without the guidance of the Holy Spirit and met fierce resistance. Not only were lives unnecessarily cut short, the Baal group then attributed the loss to a wrathful god who required the Ark of the Covenant to be present in battle.

Because of their advanced age, Moses and Aaron likely wouldn't survive to see the holy nation established. They were instructed to create a sucession plan so the experiment could continue. It would need to be public and acceptable to the Israelites to avoid causing a civil war. They named their successors; Hoshea son of Nun would become the Prophet Joshua, and Eleazar son of Aaron would become the High Priest. 

With the passing of Aaron, Eleazar was anointed as High Priest. He did little to further advance the Pillar of the Priest. His son Phineas became aligned with the Baal group, giving legitimacy to their movement. They massacred towns and villages east of the Dead Sea, and presented their success to the Israelites as evidence of divine favor. Further establishing their beliefs as authoritative. Eventually they turned their violent ideology inward, killing other Israelites to solidify power. The pinnacle act of their apostasy was the murder of the Oracle Balaam after he blessed the followers of Moses. The tribes then split into three primary clans. The clan of Joshua that remained loyal to implementing the Divine Plan. The Baal clan; a partnership between the original Israelite tribes and the priests following Phineas. And the Hebrews that chose to no longer participate, remaining east of the Jordan River. 

Ultimately, Moses failed to prevent the "Mesopotamian Problem" from overtaking the Israelites. The experiment failed to provide a foundation for the Four Pillars, but it was not a total loss. The Unity noticed that although the character of an abstract god was subject to social coercion, for a man it was much less so. Even the Baal group maintained that Moses was a prophet chosen by God to deliver them to the Promised Land. The Unity believed that the right person at the right time may still be able to save humanity. Over time, people that embody the spirit of the Pillars would emerge. They would be chosen as the Ultimate Mediators of the Divine Plan. The curated mythology of these mediators and a physical representation of the Divine Plan could become enduring memories in the Collective Spirit of humanity. Monuments to the hope God has for mankind.

Chapter 8.1
Liberation
By: Caleb son of Jephunneh 

These are the names of the sons of Israel who came to Egypt with Jacob, each with his household: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, and Benjamin, Dan and Naphtali, Gad and Asher. The total number of people born to Jacob was seventy. (Joseph was already in Egypt.) Then Joseph died, and all his brothers, and that whole generation. But the Israelites were fruitful and prolific; they multiplied and grew exceedingly strong, so that the land was filled with them. Now a new king arose over Egypt who did not know Joseph. He said to his people, “Look, the Israelite people are more numerous and more powerful than we. Come, let us deal shrewdly with them, or they will increase and, in the event of war, join our enemies and fight against us and escape from the land.” 

Therefore they set taskmasters over them to oppress them with forced labor. They built supply cities, Pithom and Rameses, for Pharaoh. The Egyptians subjected the Israelites to hard servitude and made their lives bitter with hard servitude in mortar and bricks and in every kind of field labor. They were ruthless in all the tasks that they imposed on them. Then Pharaoh commanded all his people, “Every son that is born to the Hebrews you shall throw into the Nile, but you shall let every daughter live.” Now a man from the house of Levi went and married a Levite woman. The woman conceived and bore a son, and when she saw that he was a fine baby, she hid him three months. When she could hide him no longer she got a papyrus basket for him and plastered it with bitumen and pitch; she put the child in it and placed it among the reeds on the bank of the river. 

His sister stood at a distance, to see what would happen to him. The daughter of Pharaoh came down to bathe at the river, while her attendants walked beside the river. She saw the basket among the reeds and sent her maid to bring it. When she opened it, she saw the child. He was crying, and she took pity on him. “This must be one of the Hebrews’ children,” she said. Then his sister said to Pharaoh’s daughter, “Shall I go and get you a nurse from the Hebrew women to nurse the child for you?” Pharaoh’s daughter said to her, “Yes.” So the girl went and called the child’s mother. Pharaoh’s daughter said to her, “Take this child and nurse it for me, and I will give you your wages.” So the woman took the child and nursed it. When the child grew up, she brought him to Pharaoh’s daughter, and he became her son. She named him Moses, “because,” she said, “I drew him out of the water.”

One day after Moses had grown up, he went out to his people and saw their forced labor. He saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, one of his own people. He looked this way and that, and seeing no one he killed the Egyptian and hid him in the sand. When he went out the next day, he saw two Hebrews fighting, and he said to the one who was in the wrong, “Why do you strike your fellow Hebrew?” He answered, “Who made you a ruler and judge over us? Do you mean to kill me as you killed the Egyptian?” Then Moses was afraid and thought, “Surely the thing is known.” When Pharaoh heard of it, he sought to kill Moses. So Moses fled from Pharaoh. He settled in the land of Midian and sat down by a well. 

The priest of Midian had seven daughters. They came to draw water and filled the troughs to water their father’s flock. But some shepherds came and drove them away. Moses got up and came to their defense and watered their flock. When they returned to their father Reuel, he said, “How is it that you have come back so soon today?” They said, “An Egyptian helped us against the shepherds; he even drew water for us and watered the flock.” He said to his daughters, “Where is he? Why did you leave the man? Invite him to share a meal.” Moses agreed to stay with the man, and he gave Moses his daughter Zipporah in marriage. She bore a son, and he named him Gershom, for he said, “I have been an alien residing in a foreign land.”

Moses was keeping the flock of his father-in-law Jethro, the priest of Midian; he led his flock beyond the wilderness and came to Mount Horeb, the mountain of God. There the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire out of a bush; he looked, and the bush was blazing, yet it was not consumed. Then Moses said, “I must turn aside and look at this great sight and see why the bush is not burned up.” When the Lord saw that he had turned aside to see, God called to him out of the bush, “Moses, Moses!” And he said, “Here I am.” Then he said, “Come no closer! Remove the sandals from your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground.” He said further, “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” And Moses hid his face, for he was afraid to look at God. "The cry of the Hebrews has now come to me; I have also seen how the Egyptians oppress them." 

Then the Lord said, “I have observed the misery of my people who are in Egypt; I have heard their cry on account of their taskmasters. Indeed, I know their sufferings, and I have come down to deliver them from the Egyptians and to bring them up out of that land to a good and spacious land, to a land flowing with milk and honey. Go and assemble the elders of Israel and say to them, ‘The Lord, the God of your ancestors, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, has appeared to me, saying: I have given heed to you and to what has been done to you in Egypt.' They will listen to your voice, and you and the elders of Israel shall go to the king of Egypt and say to him, ‘The Lord, the God of the Hebrews, has met with us; let us now go a three days journey into the wilderness, so that we may celebrate a festival with our Lord in the wilderness.' ” 

Then Moses said to God, “If I come to the Hebrews and say to them, ‘The God of your ancestors has sent me to you,’ and they ask me, ‘What is his name?’ what shall I say to them?” God said to Moses, “I am who I am.” He said further, “Thus you shall say to the Hebrews, ‘I AM has sent me to you.’ ” Then Moses answered, “But look, they may not believe me or listen to me but say, ‘The Lord did not appear to you.’ ” The Lord said to him, “I will be with you. Now look at the ground.” and there was a snake, and Moses drew back from it. Then the Lord said to Moses, “Reach out your hand and seize it by the tail.” So he reached out his hand and grasped it, and it became a staff in his hand. 

Again, the Lord said to him, “Put your hand inside your cloak.” He put his hand into his cloak, and when he took it out, his hand was diseased, as white as snow. Then God said, “Put your hand back into your cloak”—so he put his hand back into his cloak, and when he took it out, it was restored like the rest of his body— “If they will not believe you or heed the first sign, they may believe the second sign. If they will not believe even these two signs or listen to you, you shall take some water from the Nile and pour it on the dry ground, and the water that you shall take from the Nile will become blood on the dry ground.”

But Moses said to God, “Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the Hebrews out of Egypt? O my Lord, I have never been eloquent, neither in the past nor even now that you have spoken to your servant, but I am slow of speech and slow of tongue.” Then the Lord said to him, “Who gives speech to mortals? Who makes them mute or deaf, seeing or blind? Is it not I, the Lord? Now go, and I will be with your mouth and teach you what you are to speak. I know, however, that the king of Egypt will not let you go except by a mighty hand. When Pharaoh does not listen to you, I will lay my hand upon Egypt and bring my people, company by company, out of the land of Egypt by great acts. The Egyptians shall know that I am the Lord when I stretch out my hand against Egypt and bring my people out from among them. Then you shall say to Pharaoh, ‘Thus says the Lord: Israel is my firstborn son. I said to you, “Let my son go that he may serve me.”

Moses said, “O my Lord, please send someone else.” Then the Lord said, “What of your brother Aaron, the Levite? I know that he can speak well, and when he sees you his heart will be glad. You shall speak to him and put the words in his mouth, and I will be with your mouth and with his mouth and will teach you what you shall do." The Lord then said to Aaron, “Go into the wilderness to meet Moses.” So he went, and he met him at the mountain of God and kissed him. Moses told Aaron all the words of the Lord with which he had sent him and all the signs with which he had charged him. 

Moses went back to his father-in-law Jethro and said to him, “Please let me go back to my own people in Egypt and see whether they are still living.” And Jethro said to Moses, “Go in peace.” So Moses took his wife and his sons, put them on a donkey, and went back to the land of Egypt, and Moses carried the staff of God in his hand. On the way, at a place where they spent the night, the Holy Spirit came upon Moses and it looked as though he was going to die. But Zipporah took a flint and cut off her husband's foreskin and touched his feet with it. It was then that she said “a bridegroom of blood,” because of the circumcision. And the Lord said, "The blood shall be a sign for you on the houses where you live: when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and no plague shall destroy you when I strike the land of Egypt."

On the day when the Lord spoke to Moses in the land of Egypt, the Lord said to Moses, “Say therefore to the Hebrews: I am the Lord, and I will free you from the burdens of the Egyptians and deliver you from slavery to them. I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great acts. I will take you as my people, and I will be your God. You shall know that I am the Lord your God, who has freed you from the burdens of the Egyptians. I will bring you into the land that I swore to give to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; I will give it to you for a possession. I am the Lord.” Moses told this to the Hebrews, but they would not listen to Moses, because of their broken spirit and their cruel slavery.

Afterward Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and said, “Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: Let my people go, so that they may celebrate a festival with me in the wilderness or I will fall upon you with pestilence.” But Pharaoh said, “Who is this Lord, that I should listen to him and let the Hebrews go? I do not know this God, and I will not let Israel go. Moses and Aaron, why are you taking the people away from their work? Get to your labors!” That same day Pharaoh commanded the taskmasters of the people, as well as their supervisors, “You shall no longer give the people straw to make bricks, as before; let them go and gather straw for themselves. But you shall require of them the same quantity of bricks as they have made previously; do not diminish it, for they are lazy." 

So the people scattered throughout the land of Egypt to gather stubble for straw. And the Israelite supervisors whom Pharaoh’s taskmasters had set over them were beaten and were asked, “Why did you not finish the required quantity of bricks yesterday and today, as you did before?” Then the Israelite supervisors came to Pharaoh and cried, “Why do you treat your servants like this? No straw is given to your servants, yet they say to us, ‘Make bricks!’ Look how your servants are beaten! But the fault is with you.” He said, “You are lazy, lazy; that is why you say, ‘Let us go and worship the Lord.’ Go now and work, for no straw shall be given you, but you shall still deliver the same number of bricks.” The Israelite supervisors saw that they were in trouble when they were told, “You shall not lessen your daily number of bricks.” 

As they left Pharaoh, they came upon Moses and Aaron, who were waiting to meet them. They said to them, “The Lord look upon you and judge! You have brought us into bad odor with Pharaoh and his officials and have put a sword in their hand to kill us.” The Lord said to Moses, “Now you shall see what I will do to Pharaoh: indeed, by a mighty hand he will let them go; by a mighty hand he will drive them out of his land.” And he did so; God stretched out his hand and Moses took his staff and struck the dust of the earth, and gnats came on humans and animals alike; all the dust of the earth turned into gnats throughout the whole land of Egypt. The magicians tried to produce gnats by their secret arts, but they could not. There were gnats on both humans and animals. And the magicians said to Pharaoh, “This is the finger of God!” But Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them, just as the Lord had said. 

The Lord said to Moses in the land of Egypt, “This month shall mark for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first month of the year for you. Tell the whole congregation of Hebrews that on the evening of the tenth of this month they are to take a flint knife and circumcise the males of each household. The blood shall be a sign for you on the houses where you live: when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and no plague shall destroy you when I strike the land of Egypt. They shall take some of the blood and put it on the two doorposts and the lintel of their houses. And tell them, 'None of you shall go outside the door of your house until morning. You shall observe this as a perpetual ordinance for you and your male children. When you come to the land that the Lord will give you, as he has promised, you shall keep this observance. 

The whole congregation of Israel shall do this. If an alien who resides with you wants to celebrate the Passover of the Lord, all his males shall be circumcised; then he may draw near to celebrate it; he shall be regarded as a native of the land.' Then say to them, 'When your children ask you, What does this observance mean to you?’ you shall say, ‘It is the Passover, for the Lord passed over the houses of the Hebrews in Egypt when he struck Egypt with plagues but spared our houses.’ ” Aaron spoke all the words that the Lord had spoken to Moses and the people believed. When they heard that the Lord had given heed to the suffering of the Hebrews they bowed down and worshiped.

Then the Lord said to Moses, “Rise up early in the morning and present yourself before Pharaoh and say to him, ‘Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: Let my people go. For this time I will send all my plagues upon you yourself, your officials, and your people, so that you may know that there is no one like me in all the earth. Indeed, by now I could have stretched out my hand and struck you and your people with pestilence, and you would have been cut off from the earth. But this is why I have let you live: to show you my power and to make my name resound through all the earth. You are still exalting yourself against my people by not letting them go. Tomorrow at this time I will cause the heaviest hail to fall that has ever fallen in Egypt from the day it was founded until now. Send, therefore, and have your livestock and everything that you have in the open field brought to a secure place; every human or animal that is in the open field and is not brought under shelter will die when the hail comes down upon them.’ ” 

Those officials of Pharaoh who feared the word of the Lord hurried their slaves and livestock off to a secure place, but those who did not regard the word of the Lord left their slaves and livestock in the open field. Then the Lord rained hail on the land of Egypt; there was hail with fire flashing continually in the midst of it, such heavy hail as had never fallen in all the land of Egypt since it became a nation. The hail struck down everything that was in the open field throughout all the land of Egypt, both human and animal; the hail also struck down all the plants of the field and shattered every tree in the field. Only in the land of Goshen, where the Israelites were, was there no hail. Then Moses and Aaron went and assembled all the elders of the Israelites. 

Aaron spoke all the words that the Lord had spoken to Moses and the people believed, and when they heard that the Lord had given heed to the Israelites they bowed down and worshiped. Then Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said to them, “This time I have sinned; the Lord is in the right, and I and my people are in the wrong. Pray to the Lord! Enough of God’s thunder and hail! I will let you go; you need stay no longer.” Moses said to him, “As soon as I have gone out of the city, I will stretch out my hands to the Lord; the thunder will cease, and there will be no more hail, so that you may know that the earth is the Lord’s. But as for you and your officials, I know that you do not yet fear the Lord God.” So Moses left Pharaoh, went out of the city, and stretched out his hands to the Lord; then the thunder and the hail ceased, and the rain no longer poured down on the earth. 

But when Pharaoh saw that the rain and the hail and the thunder had ceased, he sinned once more and hardened his heart, he and his officials. So the heart of Pharaoh was hardened, and he would not let the Israelites go, just as the Lord had spoken through Moses. Then the Lord said to Moses, “Rise early in the morning and present yourself before Pharaoh, as he goes out to the water, and say to him, ‘Thus says the Lord: Let my people go, because if you will not let my people go, I will send swarms of flies on you, your officials, and your people, and into your houses. The houses of the Egyptians shall be filled with swarms of flies, as will the land where they live. But on that day I will set apart the land of Goshen, where my people live, so that no swarms of flies shall be there, that you may know that I the Lord am in this land. Thus I will make a distinction between my people and your people. This sign shall appear tomorrow.’ " 

The Lord did so, and great swarms of flies came into the house of Pharaoh and into his officials’ houses; in all of Egypt the land was ruined because of the flies. Then Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said, “Go, worship your God within the land.” But Moses said, "We must go a three days’ journey into the wilderness as the Lord our God commands us.” So Pharaoh said, “I will let you go to worship the Lord your God in the wilderness, provided you do not go very far away. Pray for me.” Then Moses said, “As soon as I leave you, I will pray to the Lord that the swarms of flies may depart tomorrow from Pharaoh, from his officials, and from his people; only do not let Pharaoh again deal falsely by not letting the people go to worship the Lord.” 

So Moses went out from Pharaoh and prayed to the Lord. And the Lord did as Moses asked: he removed the swarms of flies from Pharaoh, from his officials, and from his people; not one remained. But Pharaoh hardened his heart and would not let the people go. So Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and said to him, “Thus says the Lord, the God of the Hebrews and the Israelites: 'How long will you refuse to humble yourself before me? Let my people go. For if you refuse to let my people go, tomorrow I will bring locusts into your country. They shall cover the surface of the land, so that no one will be able to see the land. They shall devour the last remnant left you after the hail, and they shall devour every tree of yours that grows in the field. They shall fill your houses and the houses of all your officials and of all the Egyptians—something that neither your parents nor your grandparents have seen, from the day they came on earth to this day.' ” 

Then they turned and went out from Pharaoh. Later Moses and Aaron were brought back to Pharaoh, and he said to them, “Go, serve the Lord your God! But which ones are to go?” Moses said, “We will go with our young and our old; we will go with our sons and daughters and with our flocks and herds, because we have the Lord’s festival to celebrate.” He said to them, “The Lord indeed will be with you, if ever I let your little ones go with you! Plainly, you have some evil purpose in mind. No, never! Your men may go and serve the Lord, for that is what you are asking.” And they were driven out from Pharaoh’s presence. 

Then the locusts came upon all the land of Egypt and settled on the whole country of Egypt, such a dense swarm of locusts as had never been before nor ever shall be again. They covered the surface of the whole land, so that the land was black, and they ate all the plants in the land and all the fruit of the trees that the hail had left. Nothing green was left on the trees or on the plants in the fields, in all the land of Egypt. Pharaoh hurriedly summoned Moses and Aaron and said, “I have sinned against the Lord your God and against you. Do forgive my sin this once, and pray to the Lord your God that at the least he remove this deadly thing from me.” So Moses went out from Pharaoh and prayed to the Lord. The Lord lifted the locusts and drove them into the Red Sea; not a single locust was left in all the country of Egypt. 

Then Pharaoh summoned Moses and said, “Go, serve the Lord. Only your flocks and your herds shall remain behind. Even your little ones may go with you.” But Moses said, “Our livestock also must go with us; not a hoof shall be left behind, for we must choose some of them to serve the Lord our God, and we will not know what to use until we arrive there.” But Pharaoh was unwilling to let them go. Then Pharaoh’s officials said to him, “How long shall this fellow be a snare to us? Send the people away, so that they may serve the Lord their God. Do you not yet understand that Egypt is ruined?” Then Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron in the night and said, “Rise up, go away from my people, both you and the Israelites! Go, serve the Lord, as you said. Take your flocks and your herds, as you said, and be gone. Get away from me! Take care that you do not see my face again, for on the day you see my face you shall die.” Moses said, “Just as you say! I will never see your face again.” 

That very day the Lord brought Israel out of the land of Egypt, company by company. The Egyptians urged the people to hasten their departure from the land, for they said, “We shall all be dead.” So the people took their dough before it was leavened, with their kneading bowls wrapped up in their cloaks on their shoulders. And Moses took with him the bones of Joseph, who had required a solemn oath of them, saying, “God will surely come to you, and then you must carry my bones with you from here.” That was for the Lord a night of vigil, to bring them out of the land of Egypt. The Hebrews journeyed from Rameses to Succoth. A mixed crowd of Israelites also went up with them and their livestock in great numbers, both flocks and herds. They baked unleavened cakes of the dough that they had brought out of Egypt; it was not leavened, because they were driven out of Egypt and could not wait, nor had they prepared any provisions for themselves.

Aaron said to the people, “Remember this day on which you came out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery, because the Lord brought you out from there by strength of hand; no leavened bread shall be eaten. When the Lord brings you into the land of Canaan, which he swore to your ancestors to give you, a land flowing with milk and honey, you shall keep this observance in this month. Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, and on the seventh day there shall be a festival to the Lord. You shall tell your child on that day, ‘It is because of what the Lord did for me when I came out of Egypt.’ It shall serve for you as a sign on your hand and as a reminder on your forehead, so that the teaching of the Lord may be on your lips, for with a strong hand the Lord brought you out of Egypt. You shall keep this ordinance at its proper time from year to year.

When Pharaoh let the people go, God did not lead them by way of the land of the Philistines, although that was nearer, for God thought, “If the people face war, they may change their minds and return to Egypt.” So God led the people by the roundabout way of the wilderness bordering the Red Sea. The Israelites went up out of the land of Egypt prepared for battle.They set out from Succoth and camped at Etham, on the edge of the wilderness. The Lord said to Moses, “Tell the Israelite army to turn back and camp in front of Pi-hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, in front of Baal-zephon. You shall take the rest of the camp in the opposite direction and go around the sea. Pharaoh will say of the Israelites, ‘They are wandering aimlessly in the land; the wilderness has closed in on them.’ "

When the king of Egypt was told that the people had fled, the minds of Pharaoh and his officials were changed toward the people, and they said, “What have we done, letting Israel leave our service?” So he had his chariot made ready and took his army with him; he took six hundred elite chariots and all the other chariots of Egypt with officers over all of them. Then Moses ordered the congregation to set out around the Red Sea to Marah, they could not drink the water of Marah because it was bitter. Then they went into the wilderness of Shur. But the people thirsted there for water, and the people complained against Moses and said, “Why did you bring us out of Egypt, to kill us and our children and livestock with thirst?” So Moses cried out to the Lord, “What shall I do for this people? They are almost ready to stone me.”  

There the Lord made for them a statute and an ordinance, and there he put them to the test. He said, "Tell the congregation, 'If you will listen carefully to the voice of the Lord your God, and do what is right in his sight, he will not bring upon you any of the calamity that was brought upon the Egyptians, for he is the Lord who heals you.” Then they came to Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, and they camped there by the water. From Elim the congregation journeyed by stages, as the Lord commanded. They camped at Rephidim, then Amalek came and fought with Israel at Rephidim. Moses said to Joshua, “Choose some men for us and go out; fight with Amalek. Tomorrow I will stand on the top of the hill with the staff of God in my hand.” So Joshua did as Moses told him and fought with Amalek, while Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill. And Joshua defeated Amalek and his people with the sword. 

Across the Red Sea the Egyptians pursued them, all Pharaoh’s horses and chariots, his chariot drivers and his army; they nearly overtook the Israelite army camped by the sea, by Pi-hahiroth, in front of Baal-zephon. As Pharaoh drew near, the Israelites looked back, and there were the Egyptians advancing on them. In great fear the Israelites cried out to the Lord. The Angel of God who was going before the Israelite army moved and went behind them, and the pillar of cloud moved from in front of them and took its place behind them. It came between the army of Egypt and the army of Israel. And so the cloud was there with the darkness; one did not come near the other all night. Then the Lord drove the sea back and turned the sea into dry land, and the waters were divided. At the morning watch the Israelite army went into the sea on dry ground, the waters forming a wall for them on their right and on left.

In the light Moses could see the Israelite army approaching through the Red Sea, and the Egyptian army behind them. As Pharaoh drew near, the congregation with Moses looked back, and there were the Egyptians advancing on them. They said to Moses, “Was it because there were no graves in Egypt that you have taken us away to die in the wilderness? What have you done to us, bringing us out of Egypt? Is this not the very thing we told you in Egypt, ‘Let us alone so that we can serve the Egyptians’? For it would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness.”  But Moses said to the people, “Do not be afraid, stand firm, and see the deliverance that the Lord will accomplish for you today, for the Egyptians whom you see today you shall never see again. The Lord will fight for you, and you have only to keep still.” 

The Lord looked down on the Egyptian army and threw the Egyptian army into a panic. He clogged their chariot wheels so that they turned with difficulty. The Egyptians said, “Let us flee from the Israelites, for the Lord is fighting for them against Egypt.” Then the Lord said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand over the sea, so that the water may come back upon the Egyptians, upon their chariots and chariot drivers.” Israel saw the great work that the Lord did against the Egyptians. So the people feared the Lord and believed in the Lord and in his servant Moses. Then the prophet Miriam, Aaron’s sister, took a tambourine in her hand, and all the women went out after her with tambourines and with dancing. And Miriam sang to them: “Sing to the Lord, for he has triumphed gloriously; horse and rider he has thrown into the sea.”

Chapter 8.2
The Wilderness 
By: Caleb son of Jephunneh 

After the battle with Amalek, Moses had sent away his wife Zipporah, along with their two sons, and his father-in-law took her back. Then the whole congregation set out from Rephidim and came to the wilderness of Sinai, on the fifteenth day of the second month after they had departed from the land of Egypt. Now Moses used to take the tent and pitch it outside the camp, far off from the camp; he called it the Tent of Meeting. And everyone who sought the Lord would go out to the Tent of Meeting, which was outside the camp. The whole congregation of the Israelites complained against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness. The Israelites said to them, “If only we had died by the hand of the Lord in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the pots of meat and ate our fill of bread, for you have brought us out into this wilderness to kill this whole assembly with hunger.” 

The Lord spoke to Moses, “I have heard the complaining of the Israelites; say to them, ‘In the morning you shall have your fill of bread; then you shall know that I am the Lord your God.’ " Then the Lord said to Moses, “I am going to rain bread from heaven for you, and each day the people shall go out and gather enough for that day. In that way I will test them, whether they will follow my instruction or not. On the sixth day, when they prepare what they bring in, it will be twice as much as they gather on other days.” 

Then Moses said to Aaron, “Say to the whole congregation of the Israelites: ‘Draw near to the Lord, for he has heard your complaining.’ ” And as Aaron spoke to the whole congregation of the Israelites, they looked toward the wilderness, and the glory of the Lord appeared. In the evening quails came up and covered the camp. Some of the people worked all that night gathering the quails; the least anyone gathered was ten homers, and they spread them out for themselves all around the camp. But while the meat was still between their teeth, before it was consumed, the anger of the Lord was kindled against the people. 

So the Lord said to Moses, “Gather for me the elders of Israel, whom you know to be the elders of the people and officers over them; bring them to the Tent of Meeting and have them take their place there with you. I will come down and speak with you there, and I will take some of the spirit that is on you and put it on them, and they shall bear the burden of the people along with you so that you will not bear it all by yourself." So Moses went out and told the people the words of the Lord, and he gathered the elders of the people and placed them all around the tent. 

Then the Lord came down and took some of the spirit that was on him and put it on the elders, and when the spirit rested upon them, they prophesied. In the sight of the people the elders cried, "Consecrate yourselves for tomorrow you shall eat, for you have wailed in the hearing of the Lord, saying, 'If only we had bread to eat! Surely it was better for us in Egypt.' Therefore the Lord will give you bread, and you shall eat until it comes out of your nostrils and becomes loathsome to you—because you have rejected the blessing of Lord who is among you and killed the quail before him. A sickness will spread among the guilty, the ones who consumed flesh, and the Lord will not heal them of this plague.” That day the elders prophesied, but they did not do so again. So that place was called Kibroth-hattaavah, because there they buried the people who had the craving for flesh. 

In the morning there was a layer of dew around the camp. When the layer of dew lifted, there on the surface of the wilderness was a fine flaky substance, as fine as frost on the ground. When the Israelites saw it, they said to one another, “What is it?” For they did not know what it was. Moses said to them, “It is the bread that the Lord has given you to eat." The Israelites called it manna; it was like white coriander seed, and the taste of it was like wafers made with honey. Moses said to the congregation, "This is what the Lord has commanded: Gather as much of it as each of you needs, an omer per person according to the number of persons, all providing for those in their own tents.” 

Morning by morning they gathered it, as much as each needed, but when the sun grew hot, it melted. On the sixth day Moses gathered the elders and told them, “This is what the Lord has commanded: Tomorrow is a day of solemn rest, a holy Sabbath to the Lord; Six days you shall gather it, but on the seventh day, there will be none. Bake what you want to bake and boil what you want to boil, and all that is left over put aside to be kept until morning.” So they put it aside until morning, just as Moses commanded them, and it did not rot, and there were no maggots in it. On the seventh day all the leaders of the congregation came and told Moses, "Some of the people went out to gather, and they found none." And Moses said, "See! The Lord has given you the Sabbath; therefore on the sixth day he gives you food for two days; each of you stay where you are; do not leave your place on the seventh day.” So the people rested on the seventh day.

While they were traveling through the wilderness in Sinai, Miriam spoke against Moses to Aaron and said, “Has the Lord spoken only through Moses? Has he not spoken through us also?” And the Lord heard it. Now the man Moses was very humble, more so than anyone else on the face of the earth. Suddenly the Lord said to Moses, Aaron, and Miriam, “Come out, you three, to the Tent of Meeting.” So the three of them came out. And he said, “Hear my words: When there are prophets among you, I the Lord make myself known to them in visions; I speak to them in dreams. Not so with my servant Moses; he is faithful in all my house. With him I speak face to face—clearly, not in riddles, and he beholds the form of the Lord. Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant Moses?” 

And Aaron turned toward Miriam and saw that Miriam’s skin had become diseased, and was white as snow. Then Aaron said, “Oh, my lord, do not punish her for a sin that she has so foolishly committed." And Moses cried to the Lord, saying, “O God, please heal her.” But the Lord said to Moses, “Miriam defiled herself by speaking against you, therefore she spoke against me. Her heart is corrupted by the wicked spirit and there is illness in her soul. The corruption of her flesh bears the truth, she is unclean. She must repent. Let her be shut out of the camp for seven days, and after that she may be brought in again. But let the Israelites keep the Passover at its appointed time." And Miriam was shut out of the camp.

So Moses told the Israelites that they should keep the Passover. Now there were certain people who knew Miriam was unclean, and could not keep the Passover on that day. They came before Moses and said to him, “If we are unclean and repent, why must we be kept from presenting the Lord’s offering at its appointed time among the Israelites?” Moses said to them, “Wait, so that I may hear what the Lord will command concerning your query.” The Lord spoke to Moses, saying, “Speak to the Israelites, saying: Anyone of you or your descendants who is unclean and repents shall still keep the Passover to the Lord." So they kept the Passover in the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month, at twilight, in the wilderness of Sinai. Just as the Lord had commanded Moses, so the Israelites did. The people did not set out on the march until Miriam had been brought in again. 

Jethro, the priest of Midian, Moses’s father-in-law, heard of all that God had done for Moses and for his people Israel, how the Lord had brought Israel out of Egypt. He sent word to Moses, “I, your father-in-law Jethro, am coming to you, with your wife and your two sons.” So Moses went out to meet his father-in-law; he bowed down and kissed him; each asked after the other’s welfare, and they went into the tent. Then Moses told his father-in-law all that the Lord had done to Pharaoh and to the Egyptians for Israel’s sake, all the hardship that had found them on the way, and how the Lord had delivered them. Jethro rejoiced for all the good that the Lord had done to Israel, in delivering them from the Egyptians. Jethro said, “Blessed be the Lord, who has delivered you from the Egyptians and from Pharaoh. Now I know that the Lord is greater than all gods, because he delivered the people from the Egyptians, when they dealt arrogantly with them.” 

The next day Moses sat as judge for the people, while the people stood around him from morning until evening. When Moses’s father-in-law saw all that he was doing for the people, he said, “What is this that you are doing for the people? Why do you sit alone, while all the people stand around you from morning until evening?” Moses said to his father-in-law, “Because the people come to me to inquire of God. When they have a dispute, they come to me, and I decide between one person and another, and I make known to them the statutes and instructions of God.” 

Moses’s father-in-law said to him, “What you are doing is not good. You will surely wear yourself out, both you and these people with you, for the task is too heavy for you; you cannot do it alone. Now listen to me. I will give you counsel, and God be with you! You should represent the people before God and bring their cases to God. Teach them the statutes and instructions and make known to them the way they are to go and the things they are to do. You should also look for able men among all the people, men who fear God, are trustworthy, and hate dishonest gain; set them as officers over thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens. Let them sit as judges for the people at all times; let them bring every important case to you but decide every minor case themselves. So it will be easier for you, and they will bear the burden with you. If you do this and God so commands you, then you will be able to endure, and all these people will go to their homes in peace.” So Moses listened to his father-in-law and prayed for guidance.

The Lord spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, in the Tent of Meeting, on the first day of the second month, in the second year after they had come out of the land of Egypt, saying, “Take a census of the whole congregation of Israel." So Moses and Aaron went to the tribal leaders they knew by name, to assist them. And on that day they brought the whole congregation together. They assembled themselves in clans or by their ancestral houses. The divisions of the Israelites were; Levi, Judah, Ephraim and Manasseh. These were the ones chosen from the congregation, the leaders of their ancestral tribes, the heads of the divisions of Israel. The Hebrews were assembled in clans, some formed in Egypt and others on the journey. They were the generations of second sons and daughters of the ancestral houses. So they took a census of the Hebrews by their tents, and the Israelites by their ancestral houses, and enrolled all of Israel. 

Those enrolled of the tribe of Reuben were five hundred. Those enrolled of the tribe of Simeon were three hundred. Those enrolled of the tribe of Gad were six hundred fifty. Those enrolled of the tribe of Judah were six hundred. Those enrolled of the tribe of Issachar were four hundred. Those enrolled of the tribe of Zebulun were four hundred. Those enrolled of the tribe of Ephraim were five hundred. Those enrolled of the tribe of Manasseh were two hundred. Those enrolled of the tribe of Benjamin were four hundred. Those enrolled of the tribe of Dan were seven hundred. Those enrolled of the tribe of Asher were five hundred. Those enrolled of the tribe of Naphtali were four hundred. All the tents and houses numbered three thousand five hundred fifty. 

The Levites, however, were not numbered by their ancestral tribe along with them. The Lord spoke to Moses, saying, “Only the tribe of Levi you shall not enroll, and you shall not take a census of them with the others. Speak to the Hebrews and say to them: When either men or women make a special vow, the vow of a Nazirite, to separate themselves, all their days as nazirites they are holy to the Lord. The Nazirites shall be consecrated at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting. They shall shave their head and take the hair from the consecrated head and put it on the fire under the sacrifice of well-being. Then the priest shall elevate them as an elevation offering before the Lord; they are a holy portion for the priest. After that the Nazirites may be counted among the Levites." 

Moses chose able men from the Hebrews and appointed them as heads over the people, as judges over hundreds and tens, and they were named for the nine missing clans. These were their names: for the tribe of Reuben, Shammua son of Zaccur; for the tribe of Simeon, Shaphat son of Hori; for the tribe of Issachar, Igal son of Joseph; for the tribe of Benjamin, Palti son of Raphu; for the tribe of Zebulun, Gaddiel son of Sodi; for the tribe of Dan, Ammiel son of Gemalli; for the tribe of Asher, Sethur son of Michael; for the tribe of Naphtali, Nahbi son of Vophsi; for the tribe of Gad, Geuel son of Machi. And of the Israelites Moses chose from the tribe of Judah, Caleb son of Jephunneh; from the tribe of Ephraim, Hoshea son of Nun; from the tribe of Manasseh, Gaddi son of Susi. And they judged the people at all times; hard cases they brought to Moses, but any minor case they decided themselves. Now the whole congregation knew themselves as Israelites. Then Moses let his father-in-law depart, and he went off to his own country.

The Lord spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, after they had come out of the land of Egypt, saying, "Do not camp in the wilderness, bring them to me at Horeb." So Israel camped there in front of the mountain. In the morning Moses brought the people out of the camp to meet God. They took their stand at the foot of the mountain. The glory of the Lord settled on Mount Horeb, the appearance of the glory of the Lord was like a devouring fire on the top of the mountain in the sight of the Israelites. Moses said to the people, “Do not be afraid, for God has come only to test you and to put the fear of him upon you so that you do not sin.” Then God called out to Moses from the clouds. 

So Moses set out with his assistant Hoshea, and Moses went up onto the mountain of God. The Lord called to him from the mountain, “Thus you shall say to the house of Jacob and tell the Israelites: ‘You have seen what I did to the Egyptians and how I bore you on eagles’ wings and brought you to myself. Now, therefore, if you obey my voice and keep my covenant, you shall be my treasured possession out of all the peoples. Indeed, the whole earth is mine, but you shall be for me a priestly kingdom and a holy nation.’ " 

The Covenant of Israel 
Then the Lord said to Moses, “Thus you shall say to the Israelites: You have seen for yourselves how I spoke with you from heaven. In every place where I cause my name to be remembered I will come to you and bless you. You shall not make gods of silver alongside me, nor shall you make for yourselves gods of gold. You need make for me only an altar of earth and sacrifice on it your burnt offerings and your offerings of well-being, your sheep and your oxen. If anyone of the house of Israel slaughters an ox or a lamb or a goat in the camp or slaughters it outside the camp and does not bring it to the entrance of the tent of meeting, to present it as an offering before the Lord, he shall be held guilty of bloodshed; he has shed blood, and he shall be cut off from the people. If anyone of the house of Israel or of the aliens who reside among them eats any blood, I will set my face against that person who eats blood and will cut that person off from the people. You shall not make wrongful use of the name of the Lord your God, for the Lord will not acquit anyone who misuses his name. Remember the Sabbath day and keep it holy. Six days you shall labor and do all your work. But the seventh day is a Sabbath to the Lord your God; you shall not do any work. Six years you shall sow your land and gather in its yield, but the seventh year you shall let it rest and lie fallow so that the poor of your people may eat, and what they leave the wild animals may eat. You shall do the same with your vineyard and with your olive orchard. Three times in the year you shall hold a festival for me. You shall observe the Festival of Unleavened Bread; as I commanded you, you shall eat unleavened bread for seven days at the appointed time in the month of Abib, for in it you came out of Egypt. Keep the Passover at its appointed time. In the second month on the fourteenth day, at twilight, they shall keep it; they shall eat it with unleavened bread and bitter herbs. They shall leave none of it until morning nor break a bone of it; according to all the statute for the Passover they shall keep it. In the seventh month, on the tenth day of the month, atonement shall be made for you, to cleanse you; from all your sins you shall be clean before the Lord. This shall be an everlasting statute for you, to make atonement for the Israelites once in the year for all their sins. You shall humble yourselves and shall do no work, neither the native-born nor the alien who resides among you.You shall not wrong or oppress a resident alien, for you were aliens in the land of Egypt. You shall not abuse any widow or orphan. If you do abuse them, when they cry out to me, I will surely heed their cry. You shall not follow a majority in wrongdoing. You shall not join hands with the wicked to act malicious. You shall not pervert the justice due to your poor in their lawsuits. You shall take no bribe, for a bribe blinds officials and subverts the cause of those who are in the right. Keep far from a false charge, and do not kill the innocent and those in the right, for I will not acquit the guilty. I am going to send an angel in front of you, to guard you on the way and to bring you to the place that I have prepared. Be attentive to him and listen to his voice; do not rebel against him, for he will not pardon your transgression, for my name is in him."

Moses wrote down all the words of the Lord. He rose early in the morning, built an altar at the foot of the mountain, and set up twelve pillars, corresponding to the twelve tribes of Israel. Then he took the Book of the Covenant and read it in the hearing of the people, and they said, “All that the Lord has spoken we will do, and we will be obedient.” 

When Moses had told the words of the people to the Lord, the Lord said to Moses, "Thus you shall do to Aaron and to his sons, just as I have commanded you; through seven days you shall ordain them. I have called by name Bezalel son of Uri son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, and I have filled him with a divine spirit, with ability, intelligence, and knowledge, and every kind of skill, to devise artistic designs, to work in silver and bronze, and in carving wood. Moreover, I have appointed with him Oholiab son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, and I have given skill to them, so that they may make all that I will command you. Go and consecrate them today, have them wash their clothes and prepare. On the third day the Lord will come down and ordain the priests in the sight of all the people. You shall make an altar on which to offer incense; you shall make it of acacia wood. Make two silver trumpets; you shall make them of hammered work, and you shall use them for summoning the congregation and for breaking camp. When both are blown, the whole congregation shall assemble before you at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting. I will consecrate the Tent of Meeting and the altar; Aaron also and his sons I will consecrate to serve me as priests. I will dwell among the Israelites, and I will be their God. And they shall know that I am the Lord their God, who brought them out of the land of Egypt that I might dwell among them; I am the Lord their God. Now this is what you shall do to them to consecrate them to serve me as priests. You shall make a bronze basin with a bronze stand for washing. You shall put it in the Tent of Meeting before the altar, and you shall put water in it; with the water Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands and their feet. When they go into the Tent of Meeting or when they come near the altar to minister to make an offering by fire to the Lord, they shall wash with water. You shall make sacred anointing oil blended as by the perfumer; it shall be a holy anointing oil. You shall make unleavened bread, unleavened cakes mixed with oil, and unleavened wafers spread with oil. You shall make them of choice wheat flour. You shall put them in one basket and bring them to the Tent of Meeting. On the third day you shall bring Aaron and his sons to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting and wash them with water. On the fourth day you shall take the holy anointing oil and pour it on their heads and anoint them. On the fifth day you shall take the vestments and put on Aaron the robe of Joseph. On the sixth day, from the basket of unleavened bread that is before the Lord, you shall place the unleavened cakes on the palms of Aaron and the wafers on the palms of his sons and raise them as an elevation offering before the Lord. On the seventh day you shall take the cakes and wafers from their hands and turn them into smoke on the altar of incense. It is an offering by fire to the Lord. You shall bring the Levites before the tent of meeting and assemble the whole congregation of the Israelites. Take the Levites from among the Israelites and cleanse them. Thus you shall do to them, to cleanse them: sprinkle the water of purification on them; have them shave their whole body with a razor and wash their clothes and so cleanse themselves. Then you shall have the Levites stand before Aaron and his sons, and you shall present them as an elevation offering to the Lord. Thus you shall separate the Levites from among the other Israelites, and the Levites shall be mine. Thereafter the Levites may go in to do service at the Tent of Meeting, once you have cleansed them and presented them as an elevation offering. For they are unreservedly given to me from among the Israelites; I have taken them for myself, that they may do the service of the Lord. This applies to the Levites: from twenty-five years old and up they shall begin to do duty in the service of the Tent of Meeting; and from the age of fifty years they shall retire from the duty of the service and serve no more." 

As the Lord had commanded Moses concerning the Priests and Levites, so he did with them. Thereafter the Levites went in to do their service in the Tent of Meeting in attendance on Aaron and his sons. Then he said to Moses, “Come up to the Lord, you and Aaron, Hoshea and Hur, and the elders of Israel, and worship at a distance. You alone shall come near the Lord, but the others shall not come near.” Moses went up on the mountain and entered the clouds. Moses was on the mountain for forty days and forty nights. When the people saw that Moses delayed to come down from the mountain, the people gathered around the sons of Aaron and said to them, “Come, make gods for us, who shall go before us; as for this Moses, the man who brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him.” Nadab said to them, “Take off the gold rings that are on the ears of your wives, your sons, and your daughters and bring them to me.” 

So all the people took off the gold rings from their ears and brought them to Nadab. He took these from them, formed them in a mold, and cast an image of a calf, and they said, “These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt!” When Abihu saw this, he built an altar before it, and Nadab made a proclamation and said, “Tomorrow shall be a festival to the Lord.” They rose early the next day and offered burnt offerings and brought sacrifices of well-being, and the people sat down to eat and drink and rose up to revel. The Lord said to Moses, “Go down at once! Your people, whom you brought up out of the land of Egypt, have acted perversely; they have been quick to turn aside from the way that I commanded them; they have cast for themselves an image of a calf and have worshiped it and sacrificed to it and said, ‘These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt!’ ” 

Then Moses turned and went down from the mountain. When Hoshea heard the noise of the people as they shouted, he said to Moses, “There is a noise of war in the camp.” But he said, “It is not the sound made by victors or the sound made by losers; it is the sound of singing that I hear.” As soon as he came near the camp and saw the calf and the dancing, Moses’s anger burned hot, and he took the calf that they had made and threw it at the foot of the mountain.
